artifact.recommendation: Use staged canaries with automatic abort thresholds, backward-compatible additive schema changes, and pre-validated traffic reversion to the old application version. Start at 1% for at least 12 minutes, then increase through bounded stages only after error-rate and p95-latency gates pass. Automatically disable the new routing path and halt expansion on early warning; retain the old version and revert traffic immediately when database read-pattern symptoms appear.
reasoning: This option limits exposure while observing behavior that staging cannot perfectly reproduce.
A 1% canary supplies statistically useful latency data in about 12 minutes, while prior routing regressions became visible within four minutes.
Additive fields allow application rollback without a schema downgrade because the old version safely ignores them.
Automatic thresholds and feature-flag shutdown are safer than global deployment with manual monitoring.
Waiting six weeks for production-identical staging would delay the release without eliminating third-party latency variance.

The stated nine-minute global application rollback cannot by itself guarantee that customer error rate stays above 1% for no more than five minutes; rapid traffic reversion or thresholds materially below 1% are required.
considerations: Define warning thresholds below the customer limit, such as aborting on sustained error-rate elevation before it reaches 1%, with p95 latency as an independent gate.
Use stages such as 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, and 100%, shortening later observation windows only when signal volume is sufficient.
Keep old-version capacity warm throughout rollout and verify that traffic can be shifted back within the five-minute error-budget window.
Disable the routing feature first when relevant, but initiate application rollback concurrently if database read-pattern changes may be responsible.
Predefine owners, dashboards, automatic actions, and criteria for resuming after an abort.
A 12-minute initial canary plus several bounded stages can plausibly finish within one business day, but the schedule should be tested against deployment propagation times.
assumptions: The 1% canary is representative across regions, request classes, and database workloads, or can be stratified to become representative.
Automatic abort and traffic-shifting controls can react faster than the nine-minute full rollback process.
The old application version remains deployable and compatible with all writes made by the new version.
The release can remain in mixed-version operation during staged rollout.
A business day provides enough time for the proposed observation windows and global propagation.
risks: Low-volume regions or rare request paths may not be represented adequately by a global 1% sample.
Database read-pattern regressions may emerge later than the previously observed routing regressions.
A feature-flag shutdown does not reverse database access changes, so relying on it alone could violate the five-minute constraint.
If reverting customer traffic requires the full nine-minute rollback, the explicit error-rate constraint may be impossible to guarantee.
Rapid stage increases could create nonlinear load or cache effects absent at canary scale.
Automated thresholds may produce false aborts or miss failures if baselines and regional segmentation are poorly configured.
evidence_needed: Measured time to detect, decide, and shift traffic from the new version back to warm old-version capacity.
Regional and endpoint-level validation that a 1% canary provides representative error and latency signals.
Baseline variability and statistically justified abort thresholds for error rate and p95 latency.
Deployment propagation timings demonstrating that all stages can complete within one business day.
Compatibility tests covering mixed application versions, new writes, and rollback without schema downgrade.
Load-test or production-shadow evidence for nonlinear database, cache, and routing behavior at higher traffic stages.

citations.claim: The previous three routing regressions were detectable through error rate or p95 latency within four minutes.
The additive schema fields are safely ignored by the old application version, enabling rollback without schema downgrade.
A 1% canary yields statistically useful latency signals in approximately 12 minutes.
Global application rollback takes nine minutes, exceeding the five-minute customer-error allowance if rollback starts only after the limit is crossed.
Production-identical staging would take six weeks and still would not reproduce third-party latency variance.
A feature flag can disable new routing without redeployment, but database read-pattern changes require application rollback.

artifact.recommendation: Use staged canaries with automatic abort thresholds, backward-compatible additive schema changes, and a two-layer rollback plan: immediately disable the new routing path via feature flag on threshold breach, then roll back the application if database read-pattern behavior is implicated. Start at 1% for at least 12 minutes, advance through progressively larger regional or traffic stages only after error-rate and p95-latency gates pass, and complete rollout within one business day if healthy.
reasoning: A staged canary limits exposure while testing behavior that cannot be perfectly reproduced in staging.
Prior routing regressions became visible within four minutes, making automated abort thresholds suitable for meeting the five-minute incident constraint.
The 1% canary needs about 12 minutes for useful latency evidence, so each initial observation window must be at least that long rather than relying only on the four-minute historical detection time.
The additive schema is compatible with the old application, allowing application rollback without a schema downgrade.
Feature-flag shutdown provides a faster first response to routing failures than the nine-minute global application rollback.
A production-identical staging environment would delay release by six weeks and still would not reproduce an important source of production variance.
A global-at-once deployment creates unnecessary blast radius and depends on manual reaction, making compliance with the error-rate constraint less reliable.
considerations: Define automatic aborts for both customer error rate and p95 latency, with thresholds evaluated at global and canary-cohort levels.
Use minimum sample-size and sustained-window rules so low-volume noise does not cause spurious aborts while still reacting within five minutes.
Separate routing-path rollback from database-pattern rollback in runbooks and telemetry.
Pause between stages long enough to capture statistically useful signals; later high-volume stages may require shorter windows if validated by power analysis.
Prefer region-by-region or cell-by-cell progression to detect geographic and third-party latency differences while retaining unaffected control populations.
Freeze unrelated deployments during rollout and assign an incident owner with authority to stop progression.
assumptions: Disabling the routing feature flag propagates and takes effect in substantially less than five minutes.
The 1% canary represents approximately 1% of customer requests globally, so even a severe canary-local failure does not push aggregate customer error rate above 1%.
Old and new application versions can run concurrently against the additive schema.
The one-business-day target permits several gated stages totaling multiple hours.
Automatic deployment controls can halt further rollout and initiate rollback without manual approval.
risks: A database read-pattern regression cannot be fully mitigated by the routing feature flag, while full application rollback takes nine minutes.
Canary traffic may not represent particular regions, tenants, request types, or third-party latency conditions.
At larger rollout stages, a sudden regression could exceed 1% customer error rate before a nine-minute application rollback completes.
Poorly tuned latency thresholds could either miss gradual degradation or trigger false aborts.
Concurrent schema population or background jobs could introduce behavior not reversed by application rollback even though no schema downgrade is required.
evidence_needed: Measured feature-flag propagation and routing-disable time across all regions.
Exact semantics of the 1% error constraint: global aggregate, per region, per tenant, or per affected cohort.
Load-test or production-shadow evidence identifying safe abort thresholds for p95 latency and database saturation indicators.
Rollback timing by region and confirmation that rollback can begin automatically and proceed incrementally.
Statistical power analysis for every planned traffic stage and key customer segment.
Verification that all database changes, migrations, writes, and background jobs remain safe when the old application version resumes.
A tested response for database regressions that can keep customer error rate within the five-minute limit despite a nine-minute global rollback.

citations.claim: The previous three routing regressions were detectable through error rate or p95 latency within four minutes.
The schema fields are additive and safely ignored by the old application version, supporting rollback without schema downgrade.
A 1% canary yields statistically useful latency signals in about 12 minutes.
Global application rollback takes nine minutes.
Production-identical staging would take six weeks and would still miss third-party latency variance.
The routing path can be disabled without redeployment, but database read-pattern changes require application rollback.

strengths: Selects the staged-canary option and clearly explains why it limits blast radius under imperfect staging fidelity.
Correctly uses the 12-minute evidence requirement for the initial 1% latency canary rather than treating the historical four-minute detection time as sufficient.
Provides a practical two-layer response: feature-flag disablement for routing failures and application rollback for database read-pattern failures.
Correctly connects additive, backward-compatible schema fields to rollback without schema downgrade.
Explicitly identifies the nine-minute application rollback as a conflict risk with the five-minute error-rate constraint.
Rejects global-at-once deployment and indefinite staging delay using evidence directly supplied in the problem.
Separates cited evidence, assumptions, risks, and further evidence needed, making uncertainty unusually transparent.
Includes regional progression, control populations, deployment freeze, ownership, sample-size rules, and database saturation telemetry.
weaknesses: The recommendation is more definitive than its own evidence supports because essential safety conditions—feature-flag propagation time and exact error-budget semantics—remain unverified.
It does not provide a concrete stage schedule, traffic percentages, dwell times, promotion criteria, or rollback triggers demonstrating completion within one business day.
The phrase "automatic abort thresholds" conflates stopping progression, disabling a feature, and initiating application rollback, which have different effects and response times.
Historical detection within four minutes leaves little or no time for threshold evaluation, flag propagation, or mitigation before the five-minute limit.
The proposed minimum-sample and sustained-window rules are not reconciled quantitatively with the requirement to react within five minutes.
It recommends automatic application rollback without showing that automation is available, safe, or capable of improving the stated nine-minute completion time.
The latency gate is underspecified: no baseline-relative threshold, regional treatment, saturation metric, or false-positive policy is given.
unsupported: The claim that feature-flag shutdown is a sufficiently fast first response is conditional on an unmeasured propagation and effect time.

The assumption that a 1% canary cannot drive aggregate error rate above 1% is not guaranteed: traffic weighting, retries, shared-resource failures, and spillover can make impact exceed nominal canary allocation.
Concurrent operation of old and new application versions against the additive schema is plausible but not fully established by evidence that old code merely ignores new fields.
The ability of deployment controls to halt, disable routing, and initiate rollback automatically is not stated in the supplied evidence.
The assertion that later stages may safely use shorter windows requires stage-specific power analysis that the report correctly requests but does not provide.
Completion within one business day is asserted as a target but not demonstrated with a rollout timeline.
missing: A precise definition of the 1% error-rate constraint, including scope, measurement window, denominator, and whether it applies globally, regionally, per tenant, or per cohort.
Explicit numeric abort thresholds and evaluation logic for error rate, p95 latency, database saturation, and data-integrity signals.
A stage-by-stage rollout plan with percentages or regions, observation durations, promotion gates, cumulative timing, and maximum permitted exposure.
A control strategy for shared dependencies where a canary can degrade non-canary traffic through database contention, cache effects, connection pools, or third-party limits.

A mitigation that can satisfy the five-minute constraint for database regressions despite a nine-minute global rollback, such as regional rollback timing, read-pattern kill switches, or capacity safeguards.
Validation of feature-flag behavior during control-plane failure, including propagation lag, stale configuration, and regional inconsistency.
Data correctness and integrity monitoring; error rate and p95 latency alone may not reveal incorrect routing, stale reads, or malformed database access.
A clear rule preventing promotion when telemetry is incomplete, delayed, or contradictory.
Rollback rehearsal results and confirmation that rollback itself does not overload the database or create mixed-version incompatibilities.
incorrect_assumptions: Detectability within four minutes is implicitly treated as supporting compliance with a five-minute incident limit, but detection is not remediation and leaves at most one minute for action.
A nominally 1% canary is assumed to cap customer impact near 1%, overlooking shared-resource and cascading failures.

Additive fields and old-version field ignorance are treated as sufficient evidence of complete mixed-version database safety, although writes, migrations, indexes, background jobs, and changed query behavior may still be incompatible.
The one-business-day rollout target is assumed to accommodate multiple gated stages without a calculated schedule.
Automatic controls are assumed to exist and operate without manual approval even though this is not provided in the problem evidence.
critical_risks: A database read-pattern regression may violate the five-minute error-rate limit because the only stated effective mitigation—application rollback—takes nine minutes globally.
A canary can affect shared database or third-party resources and harm traffic outside the canary, invalidating blast-radius assumptions.
An unmeasured feature-flag propagation delay could make the routing-layer response too slow to meet the constraint.
Ambiguous error-budget semantics could result in a policy that appears compliant globally while violating regional, tenant, or cohort limits.

A 12-minute observation period may be statistically necessary for latency but cannot justify allowing a known error-rate breach to persist; separate immediate safety and statistical promotion gates are essential.
Lack of data-integrity gates could permit a release that is latency-healthy and low-error but functionally incorrect.
recommended_changes: Make the recommendation conditional: do not begin rollout until feature-flag propagation, automatic stop behavior, mixed-version safety, and the scope of the 1% constraint are verified.
Define separate gates: an immediate safety abort for error-rate or integrity breaches and a longer statistical promotion gate for latency evidence.

Specify a concrete rollout sequence—for example 1%, then bounded regional or cell stages—with exact dwell times, promotion criteria, maximum stage size, and a timeline proving one-business-day completion.
Require feature-flag propagation and mitigation to complete with enough margin before five minutes; otherwise add a faster routing kill mechanism.
Do not increase traffic until a tested database-regression mitigation can constrain impact within five minutes despite the nine-minute global rollback time.
Add database health and correctness indicators such as query latency, saturation, connection exhaustion, lock contention, replica lag, retry amplification, and read-result validation.
Model and test shared-resource spillover so canary allocation is not treated as a hard bound on affected traffic.
Clarify that automatic abort must stop promotion immediately, disable routing when applicable, and start scoped application rollback when database indicators fire.
Require fail-closed behavior when telemetry is missing or delayed and preserve unaffected control populations throughout rollout.
Document and rehearse rollback under mixed-version, partial-region, control-plane-failure, and peak-load conditions before release.

strengths: Selects the staged-canary option and directly ties it to the release’s production-only uncertainty and high-risk profile.
Correctly recognizes that additive, backward-compatible schema changes satisfy the no-schema-downgrade rollback constraint.
Identifies the central safety conflict: a nine-minute application rollback cannot, by itself, enforce the five-minute customer error-rate limit.
Distinguishes routing failures, which feature flags can mitigate, from database read-pattern failures, which require application rollback.
Uses the supplied evidence accurately and provides traceable citations for the major claims.
Explicitly calls for automatic gates, warm rollback capacity, mixed-version compatibility testing, ownership, dashboards, and regional segmentation.
Acknowledges canary blind spots, delayed database regressions, nonlinear scale effects, and threshold-quality risks.
weaknesses: The proposed policy remains partly qualitative: it does not specify exact abort thresholds, evaluation windows, baseline comparisons, or regional versus global aggregation rules.
The stage sequence of 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, and 100% is illustrative but not justified by the evidence or a quantified exposure analysis.

It recommends immediate traffic reversion and concurrent rollback without presenting evidence that the deployment architecture supports version-based traffic shifting independently of the nine-minute rollback.
The completion-within-one-business-day claim is only described as plausible and is not demonstrated with a rollout timeline.
The report does not clearly separate mandatory launch prerequisites from follow-up evidence that could be collected during rollout.
unsupported: The claim that rapid traffic reversion can keep impact within five minutes is unsupported; only the nine-minute global application rollback time is given.
The assumption that old-version capacity can remain warm and receive shifted traffic is not established by the problem evidence.
The assumption that mixed-version operation is safe is plausible but not proven by additive-field compatibility alone; write semantics and database access interactions remain unverified.
The suggested percentage stages and shortening of later observation windows lack statistical or operational support.
The claim that the rollout can plausibly finish within one business day is unsupported without propagation times, per-stage hold periods, and abort/retry allowances.
Prior routing regressions being detectable within four minutes does not establish equally fast detection for the new database read-pattern risks.
missing: A precise control policy defining warning, abort, and rollback triggers for error rate and p95 latency, including duration, minimum sample size, and baseline comparison.
A regional rollout design that prevents a global 1% sample from masking failures in low-volume regions or specific request classes.
An explicit feasibility determination for the five-minute constraint when a database regression requires a nine-minute rollback.
A contingency policy if fast version-based traffic reversion is unavailable, such as limiting initial exposure further or treating that capability as a release blocker.
A quantified schedule showing that all observation windows and global deployment propagation fit within one business day.
Database-specific leading indicators such as query latency, connection saturation, lock contention, replica lag, and pool exhaustion.
Clear criteria for pausing versus rolling back, declaring rollback complete, resuming after an abort, and handling partial regional failures.
Validation that rollback capacity, traffic controls, telemetry, and automation remain functional during a regional or control-plane impairment.
incorrect_assumptions: It implicitly treats additive schema compatibility as sufficient proof that every write and mixed-version interaction is rollback-safe; the evidence only states that the old application ignores the new fields safely.
It assumes automatic controls can react and shift traffic faster than the documented nine-minute rollback, although that capability is listed only as an assumption and evidence need.
It assumes a 1% canary can be made representative across regions, endpoints, and database workloads without evidence that traffic allocation supports such stratification.
It assumes the five-minute constraint can be guaranteed by thresholds below 1%; early thresholds reduce risk but cannot guarantee compliance under abrupt or fast-growing failures.
critical_risks: A database read-pattern regression could push customer errors above 1% and remain there longer than five minutes because the only evidenced application rollback takes nine minutes.
A global aggregate gate could pass while a particular region, tenant, endpoint, or database shard experiences severe failure.
Scaling from a small canary may trigger nonlinear database, cache, connection-pool, or routing effects that were absent at 1%.
An unvalidated traffic-reversion mechanism could fail at the exact moment it is needed, leaving the rollout unable to satisfy the explicit safety constraint.
Poorly calibrated automation could either permit harmful expansion or repeatedly abort healthy stages, threatening both safety and the one-business-day objective.
recommended_changes: Make verified sub-five-minute version-based traffic reversion to warm old capacity a release prerequisite; if unavailable, explicitly state that the five-minute constraint cannot be guaranteed for database regressions.
Define concrete, statistically justified gates for global and per-region error rate, p95 latency, and database health, with evaluation windows and minimum sample sizes.
Specify stratified canaries by region, request class, endpoint, and database workload instead of relying on an undifferentiated global 1% sample.
Provide a timed rollout schedule, including propagation and observation periods, demonstrating whether the one-business-day requirement is achievable.
Add mandatory mixed-version, write-compatibility, rollback, and traffic-shift drills before production rollout.
Justify stage sizes using blast-radius and signal-volume calculations, and require longer holds at stages where nonlinear load effects become plausible.

State the decision rule unambiguously: routing-only symptoms trigger immediate flag disable and rollout halt; database or ambiguous symptoms trigger immediate traffic reversion and application rollback.
Separate launch blockers from desirable evidence so operators know which validations must pass before rollout begins.

attacks: The staged-canary recommendation is not yet a feasible policy: its only evidenced remedy for database read-pattern failures takes nine minutes, directly conflicting with the five-minute limit.

The argument overgeneralizes from three routing regressions to a release that also changes database access patterns; those observations provide little evidence about database failure detection latency.
A nominal 1% canary does not bound impact to 1% because database contention, retry amplification, cache disruption, and third-party saturation can spill into control traffic.
Additive fields and old-code field ignorance do not prove rollback safety for writes, indexes, migrations, background jobs, query semantics, or mixed-version behavior.
The proposed fast traffic reversion, warm old-version capacity, automatic rollback, and sub-five-minute flag propagation are assumed capabilities, not supplied facts.
Thresholds below 1% reduce expected risk but cannot guarantee compliance when failures are abrupt, telemetry is delayed, or mitigation takes longer than the remaining margin.
The 12-minute latency sampling window conflicts with rapid safety enforcement unless immediate error and integrity aborts are explicitly separated from statistical promotion gates.
The suggested stage sizes and shorter later holds are unsupported and may skip the traffic levels where nonlinear database or cache effects emerge.
Global error and latency gates could conceal severe regional, tenant, endpoint, or shard-level failures.
Completion within one business day is asserted without deployment propagation times, stage dwell calculations, rollback drills, or allowance for false aborts.
falsifiers: A production drill shows that database-regression symptoms cannot be detected and customer traffic restored to the old version within five minutes; this falsifies compliance of the proposed policy.
Shadow or canary testing shows measurable degradation in non-canary traffic through shared database, cache, connection-pool, or third-party resources; this falsifies the assumed blast-radius bound.
Stratified analysis shows that a global 1% sample lacks sufficient volume or representation for any critical region, tenant, endpoint, or database workload.
Mixed-version and rollback tests reveal incompatible writes, changed read semantics, unsafe background jobs, or persistent effects after reverting the application.
Feature-flag tests under regional or control-plane impairment exceed the mitigation-time budget or produce inconsistent routing behavior.
Load tests show a regression appearing only above a later traffic threshold, invalidating conclusions drawn from the 1% canary.
Telemetry fault tests show delayed, missing, or contradictory signals can permit promotion or postpone abort beyond the safety window.
A fully timed rehearsal shows the required stages and statistically justified dwell periods cannot complete within one business day.
Clarification that the 1% limit applies per region, tenant, or affected cohort—rather than globally—could invalidate the proposed aggregation and canary policy.
evidence_gaps: Exact semantics of the 1% constraint: scope, denominator, evaluation window, and treatment of retries and partial cohorts.
Measured detection-to-mitigation time for database regressions, including telemetry delay, decision latency, traffic shift, and recovery confirmation.
Evidence that version-based traffic reversion exists independently of the nine-minute deployment rollback and works globally within five minutes.
Measured feature-flag propagation and effectiveness across regions, including stale configuration and control-plane failure.
Concrete warning, abort, and rollback thresholds for error rate, latency, correctness, and database saturation, with baseline and minimum-sample rules.
Stage-specific statistical power and representativeness across regions, request classes, tenants, endpoints, and database workloads.
Tests for shared-resource spillover, retry amplification, nonlinear scale effects, and failures that appear only at larger stages.
Mixed-version compatibility evidence covering writes, migrations, indexes, background jobs, query behavior, and rollback under peak load.
Data-integrity and functional-correctness signals capable of detecting failures that error rate and p95 latency miss.
A stage-by-stage schedule with propagation times, dwell periods, promotion gates, maximum exposure, and proof of one-business-day completion.
Fail-closed behavior when telemetry or automation is unavailable, plus rehearsals under partial-region and control-plane failures.

accepted_criticisms: The staged-canary recommendation was not operationally feasible as stated because database read-pattern failures require a nine-minute rollback, while the constraint permits error above 1% for at most five minutes.
Evidence from three routing regressions does not establish detection latency for database read-pattern regressions.
A 1% traffic canary does not necessarily limit total customer impact to 1% because shared database, cache, connection-pool, retry, and third-party effects can spill into control traffic.

Additive fields safely ignored by old code establish limited schema compatibility, not complete rollback safety for writes, migrations, indexes, background jobs, query semantics, or mixed-version behavior.
Fast version-based traffic reversion, warm old-version capacity, and sub-five-minute automated mitigation were unsupported assumptions and must be validated prerequisites.
Thresholds below 1% reduce risk but cannot guarantee the five-minute constraint under abrupt failures, delayed telemetry, or slow mitigation.
The report did not clearly separate immediate safety aborts from the 12-minute statistical latency gate used for promotion.
The proposed stage sizes and shorter later holds were illustrative and unsupported, especially given nonlinear database and cache risks.
Global gates can mask severe failures affecting particular regions, tenants, endpoints, workloads, or shards.
Completion within one business day was not demonstrated with propagation times, dwell periods, rollback drills, or abort allowances.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Choose staged canaries only conditionally. Treat verified detection and restoration of customer traffic to the old application version within five minutes—including database-regression scenarios—as a mandatory release prerequisite. Also require mixed-version and rollback safety tests, stratified regional/workload gates, shared-resource spillover tests, fail-closed telemetry and automation, justified stage sizes and holds, and a timed one-business-day rehearsal. If sub-five-minute restoration cannot be demonstrated, none of the listed options satisfies all constraints as written; do not release until the rollback capability or constraint is changed.
reasons: Staged canaries remain safer than a global manual deployment and more informative than waiting six weeks for imperfect staging.
The only evidenced remedy for database read-pattern changes is a nine-minute application rollback, which cannot itself satisfy the five-minute safety requirement.
The prior report identified this conflict but still recommended an unproven traffic-reversion capability instead of making it an explicit launch blocker.
The supplied evidence supports schema-downgrade avoidance only narrowly and does not prove complete application or data rollback safety.
A compliant policy requires measured end-to-end detection, decision, traffic restoration, and recovery confirmation—not merely early thresholds or a nominally small canary.
The business-day objective and statistical promotion gates remain achievable possibilities, but feasibility must be established by a fully timed rehearsal.

accepted_criticisms: The recommendation was too definitive because the only evidenced mitigation for database read-pattern failures is a nine-minute application rollback, which cannot by itself ensure compliance with the five-minute error-rate limit.
Evidence from three routing regressions does not establish detection or mitigation latency for database regressions.
A nominal 1% canary does not guarantee that only 1% of traffic is affected because shared-resource contention, retries, caches, and third parties can create spillover.
Additive fields safely ignored by old code establish only limited schema compatibility, not full mixed-version or rollback safety for writes, migrations, indexes, jobs, or query semantics.
Fast feature-flag propagation, automatic controls, warm rollback capacity, and sub-five-minute mitigation were assumptions rather than supplied facts.
Immediate safety aborts must be separated from the 12-minute statistical latency promotion window.
Global gates are insufficient without regional, tenant, endpoint, shard, database-health, and integrity signals.
The report did not demonstrate that the rollout stages and dwell periods could complete within one business day.
The policy needs fail-closed behavior for missing or delayed telemetry and testing for shared-resource spillover and nonlinear failures at larger stages.
rejected_criticisms: The report did not claim that thresholds below 1% guarantee compliance; it explicitly identified abrupt larger-stage regressions and the nine-minute rollback as risks.
The report did not prescribe unsupported exact later-stage sizes, and it made shorter later holds conditional on validated power analysis.
Choosing staged canaries over global deployment or waiting six weeks remains directionally correct; the flaw was presenting rollout as ready before its safety prerequisites were verified.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Select the staged-canary option only conditionally, and do not begin production rollout until the 1% constraint is precisely defined and rehearsals demonstrate that routing and database regressions can be detected and customer impact constrained within five minutes. Require separate immediate error/integrity abort gates and longer statistical promotion gates, verified feature-flag propagation, fail-closed telemetry, mixed-version database safety, spillover/load testing, scoped rollback behavior, and a timed stage schedule proving one-business-day completion. If no database-regression mitigation can satisfy the five-minute limit despite the nine-minute global rollback, the release must remain blocked or be redesigned with a database read-pattern kill switch or faster scoped rollback.
reasons: The original option selection was the least risky of the three choices, but the recommended policy was not presently feasible under the stated hard constraint.
The nine-minute rollback is direct evidence of a compliance gap for database failures, while no faster database mitigation is provided.
The routing feature flag cannot mitigate database read-pattern changes, and its own propagation time is unmeasured.
The 12-minute latency window is suitable for promotion evidence but cannot govern response to an active five-minute error-limit breach.
Backward-compatible additive fields support rollback without schema downgrade but do not prove complete operational rollback safety.
A conditional, test-gated recommendation preserves the benefits of canaries without asserting unsupported safety or schedule guarantees.

artifact.decision: Choose staged canaries conditionally, but block the release until a tested mitigation can restore customer traffic to the old application version within five minutes for database read-pattern failures. If that capability cannot be demonstrated, none of the listed options satisfies all constraints as written.
artifact.action: Require a timed production-like rehearsal covering database regressions, shared-resource spillover, mixed-version behavior, telemetry failure, and rollback. Proceed only if it proves sub-five-minute detection and restoration, safe rollback without schema downgrade, stratified gates, and completion within one business day.
reasons: Staged canaries are directionally safer than a global manual deployment and provide production evidence that imperfect staging cannot supply.
The only evidenced mitigation for database read-pattern changes is a nine-minute application rollback, conflicting with the five-minute error-rate constraint.
The routing feature flag does not mitigate database read-pattern changes, and no faster version-reversion capability is established.
A 12-minute canary window supports latency-based promotion decisions but cannot serve as the response window for an active safety breach.
Additive fields safely ignored by old code support schema compatibility narrowly, but do not establish complete mixed-version or rollback safety.
Waiting six weeks for production-identical staging would neither meet the intended schedule nor eliminate third-party latency variance.
evidence: Problem e4 states that global application rollback completes in nine minutes.
Problem e6 states that database read-pattern changes require application rollback, while the feature flag only disables the new routing path.
Problem e3 states that a 1% canary needs about 12 minutes for statistically useful latency signals.
Problem e1 covers only three prior routing regressions detected within four minutes; it provides no corresponding database-regression evidence.
Problem e2 states only that new fields are additive and safely ignored by the old application.
Problem e5 states that production-identical staging would take six weeks and still miss third-party latency variance.
rejected_alternatives: Reject global-at-once deployment with manual monitoring because it maximizes blast radius and supplies no credible way to satisfy the five-minute constraint.
Reject unconditional staged deployment because its essential database mitigation is slower than the hard limit and faster traffic reversion is unproven.
Reject waiting specifically for a production-identical staging environment because it takes six weeks and still cannot reproduce all relevant production variance.
Reject treating a nominal 1% canary as a guaranteed 1% impact cap because shared dependencies and retries can affect control traffic.
minority: A staged canary remains the preferred architecture if its launch prerequisites are verified; the decision is not a categorical rejection of that option.
The one-business-day objective may be achievable, but the artifacts do not contain a timed schedule proving it.
unresolved: The scope, denominator, and evaluation window of the 1% error-rate constraint are undefined.
No measured end-to-end detection-to-restoration time exists for database regressions.
Feature-flag propagation time and behavior during regional or control-plane failures are unknown.
Mixed-version safety for writes, migrations, indexes, jobs, and changed query semantics is unproven.
Stage sizes, dwell periods, stratification, promotion gates, and business-day timing are unspecified.
The availability of warm old-version capacity and independent version-based traffic shifting is unestablished.
assumptions: The five-minute requirement is a hard operational constraint rather than a best-effort objective.
Application rollback is the only supplied effective mitigation for database read-pattern failures.
No unstated traffic-management capability should receive evidentiary credit.
A conditional selection is permissible even though the listed staged-canary option does not enumerate every prerequisite.
change_conditions: Approve rollout if rehearsals demonstrate reliable database-regression detection and customer-traffic restoration within five minutes under peak load and partial failures.
Approve rollout only after mixed-version and rollback tests establish safe writes, jobs, migrations, indexes, and query behavior.
Revise the decision if the 1% constraint is clarified in a way that materially changes acceptable exposure or mitigation timing.
Keep the release blocked if mitigation depends on the documented nine-minute rollback or if spillover affects non-canary traffic.
Redesign the release with a database read-pattern kill switch or faster scoped rollback if sub-five-minute restoration cannot otherwise be achieved.
next_validation: Define the exact 1% metric, scope, denominator, retry treatment, and measurement window.
Run timed database-regression drills measuring telemetry delay, decision latency, traffic restoration, and recovery confirmation.
Test canary spillover through databases, caches, connection pools, retries, and third parties at increasing traffic levels.
Validate stratified error, latency, integrity, and database-health gates with fail-closed behavior for missing telemetry.
Rehearse mixed-version operation and rollback under peak load, regional impairment, and control-plane failure.
